article_title: CHAPTER 8 ‒ Assessing Persistence in Educational Games
citation: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games
title: GIFT Gateway Module for real-time persistence assessment across game-based learning environments
description: The Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT) supports open and dynamic game-based learning environments with distinct messaging protocols. To detect persistence regardless of the educational game used, "a 'Gateway Module ' is incorporated that associates an external educational/training system 's state data with a domain or competency model built within GIFT." This linkage lets disparate systems communicate, enabling real-time assessment of persistence in players, with progress communicated to the learner model for determining transitions in performance or competency and to the pedagogical model for selecting feedback and remediation tactics.
requirements: GIFT requires rules and models built around game interaction that must be explicitly linked to concepts defined inside of the GIFT architecture
target_learners: learners in game-based training and educational environments
target_learning_goals: real-time stealth assessment of persistence and performance transitions in game-based learning
examples: The chapter describes embedding persistence detection within GIFT's domain module so it applies regardless of the educational game being utilized
key_sources: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games

article_title: Dimensional comparisons in students' perceptions of the learning environment
citation: Arens, A.K., & Möller, J. (2016). Dimensional comparisons in students' perceptions of the learning environment. Learning and Instruction, 42, 22–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.001
title: The generalized internal/external frames of reference (GI/E) model extends the classic I/E model and dimensional comparison theory to outcome variables beyond academic self-concepts.
description: The GI/E model generalizes the internal/external frames of reference model, which explains near-zero correlations between math and language self-concepts via simultaneous social and dimensional comparisons. Building on dimensional comparison theory, the GI/E model assumes "dimensional comparisons to become evident by negative or near-zero cross-domain relations between any kinds of independent and outcome variables." This study applies the model to students' perceptions of the learning environment — perceived instructional quality and student-teacher relations — as outcome variables, finding the predicted pattern of positive within-domain and negative or near-zero cross-domain relations with achievement.
requirements: Requires at least two domains with comparable achievement and outcome measures to test cross-domain versus within-domain relations
constraints: The classic I/E model was restricted to math and language achievement as independent variables and self-concepts as outcomes; the GI/E model opens this logic to other variables but the present evidence is limited to achievement as the independent variable
target_learners: elementary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: understanding how social and dimensional comparison processes shape students' perceptions of their learning environment
examples: The study tested the GI/E model with N = 4926 students, using math and language grades as achievement indicators and four-item scales for perceived teacher relations and instructional quality in each domain.
key_sources: Arens, A.K., & Möller, J. (2016). Dimensional comparisons in students' perceptions of the learning environment. Learning and Instruction, 42, 22–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.001

article_title: Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research
citation: Robert A. Sottilare, Ryan S. Baker, Arthur C. Graesser, & James C. Lester. (2017). Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0149-9
title: GIFT: a generalized framework for building intelligent tutoring systems with authoring, instructional management, and evaluation functions
description: GIFT is a research prototype ITS framework sponsored by the US Army Research Laboratory, described as a 'generalized framework for building ITSs' in the shell-tutor tradition. It ties together models of learners, instruction, and knowledge/skill domains through three functions: authoring, instructional management, and evaluation. Its stated design goals are to lower authoring skills/time, deliver adaptive instruction tailored to individual learners or teams, and provide tools to evaluate ITS effectiveness. The framework is grounded in learning, tutoring, and motivational theory and is released as free software.
requirements: Software, documentation, and technical papers are accessed via www.GIFTtutoring.org; the framework supports integration of external environments through a standardized gateway
constraints: Described as a research prototype rather than a production system; its design goals are stated as aspirations being realized progressively
target_learners: Individual learners and teams of learners in military and civilian training domains
target_learning_goals: Adaptive instruction across cognitive, affective, psychomotor, and social domains
examples: GIFT authoring tools interface with games (e.g., Virtual BattleSpace, Virtual Medic), simulations, applications, and physiological/behavioral sensors via a standard gateway specification
key_sources: Robert A. Sottilare, Ryan S. Baker, Arthur C. Graesser, & James C. Lester. (2017). Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0149-9

article_title: Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research
citation: Robert A. Sottilare, Ryan S. Baker, Arthur C. Graesser, & James C. Lester. (2017). Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0149-9
title: GIFT authoring tools with standard gateway for external environments and drag-and-drop course objects
description: GIFT's authoring function provides policies, tools, and methods enabling authors (instructional designers, developers, instructors, course managers, and subject matter experts) to create ITSs without programming knowledge, curate content across cognitive, affective, psychomotor, and social domains, and sequence it by hierarchical or dependency relationships. A 'standard gateway specification for interacting with all types of external environments' lets course objects interface with games, simulations, applications, and sensors, and course objects 'require no programming and may be added to a GIFT-based tutor through a simple drag and drop.' GIFT is also LTI compliant for MOOC delivery platforms.
requirements: New games, simulations, applications, and sensors can be added with minor programming to define enumerations as public classes of information available to GIFT for assessment
constraints: Adding new external environments beyond existing interfaces requires minor programming to define enumerations
target_learners: Authors including instructional designers, developers, instructors/teachers, course managers, and subject matter experts
target_learning_goals: Lowering the skills and time required to author ITSs in a variety of task domains
examples: Course objects interface with Virtual BattleSpace, Virtual Medic, an excavator simulator, Microsoft PowerPoint, Zephyr Bioharness, Microsoft Kinect, and Emotiv Epoc EEG
key_sources: Robert A. Sottilare, Ryan S. Baker, Arthur C. Graesser, & James C. Lester. (2017). Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0149-9

article_title: Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research
citation: Robert A. Sottilare, Ryan S. Baker, Arthur C. Graesser, & James C. Lester. (2017). Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0149-9
title: GIFT evaluation testbed methodology for experimentally assessing ITS technologies
description: GIFT's evaluation function serves as a testbed, derived from Hanks et al. (1993), supporting manipulation of the learner model, instructional strategies, and domain-specific knowledge within GIFT. It enables researchers to experimentally assess ITS components, tools, and methods and their effect on engagement, knowledge or skill acquisition, retention, reasoning, and transfer of skills. The methodology supports observation and classification of agent behaviors in an exploratory phase using educational data mining, stricter hypothesis-testing comparisons in a confirmatory phase, and replication of conditions and measurement to generalize results.
requirements: Experiment authors must be able to define measurement and assessment methods to discern learner states and record contextual data during evaluations
constraints: Generalization of results requires replication of conditions and associated measurement to be possible
target_learners: ITS researchers evaluating adaptive instructional methods and technologies
target_learning_goals: Evaluating effects of instructional tools, models, and methods on engagement, learning, performance, retention, reasoning, and transfer
examples: Figure 1 illustrates the analysis testbed methodology implemented in GIFT to support experimentation
key_sources: Robert A. Sottilare, Ryan S. Baker, Arthur C. Graesser, & James C. Lester. (2017). Special Issue on the Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT): Creating a Stable and Flexible Platform for Innovations in AIED Research. article_title: Modeling Expert Behavior in Support of an Adaptive Psychomotor Training Environment: a Marksmanship Use Case
citation: Goldberg, B., Amburn, C., Ragusa, C., & Chen, D. (2018). Modeling Expert Behavior in Support of an Adaptive Psychomotor Training Environment: a Marksmanship Use Case. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:194–224. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0155-y
title: GIFT-based methodology for building generalized expert models of psychomotor skill for adaptive tutoring
description: The article presents a methodology for extending intelligent tutoring systems into psychomotor domains, using GIFT (Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring) to sync sensor data from a marksmanship simulator and a wearable breathing sensor. It holds that a psychomotor ITS requires, at a minimum, "data types at a granular enough level to inform appropriate assessments", "established models of expert performance to inform performance state determinations", and "a pedagogical model that guides practice and accelerates skill acquisition through formative feedback and adaptive sequencing". Expert models are built bottom-up from sensor data to complement top-down doctrinal task descriptions, and serve as AI assessment criteria driving a self-regulated training environment.
requirements: Sensor technologies that capture behavioral data at a granular level without hindering task-related movements
Expert performance data from top performers to build models
A pedagogical model for formative feedback and adaptive sequencing
constraints: Models in this work cover only trigger squeeze, breath control, and body stability; aiming assessment is deferred to future work
Validation of the approach in psychomotor domains requires further work to confirm diagnostic sensitivity
target_learners: Novice soldiers learning rifle marksmanship
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill acquisition in rifle marksmanship fundamentals
examples: Eight U.S. Army Marksmanship Unit Service Rifle Team members fired five-shot groups in four stance/gear conditions while GIFT logged time-synced simulator and breathing sensor data
key_sources: Goldberg, B., Amburn, C., Ragusa, C., & Chen, D. (2018). Modeling Expert Behavior in Support of an Adaptive Psychomotor Training Environment: a Marksmanship Use Case. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:194–224. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0155-y

article_title: Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture
citation: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y
title: GIFT (Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring) adapted for team tutoring via hierarchical DKFs and team models
description: GIFT is an open-source architecture for authoring, delivering, managing, and evaluating ITS, composed of modules (Sensor, Learner, Pedagogical, Domain) that interact through standardized messages. The article describes modifications needed for team tutoring: authoring tools that define "team concepts, conditions, scenarios, individual roles, responsibilities, and assessments", hierarchical Domain Knowledge Files (one DKF per team member and one for the team), and a Team Model assessing team states such as performance, cohesion, and coaching/leadership. Its distributed architecture allows each learner's tutor to share individual state changes with other tutoring agents, supporting both team-level and individual learner models.
requirements: The article states the current GIFT structure (version 2016-1) "cannot provide collective tutoring sufficiently without significant modification"
A method must be developed to link responsibilities to individual team members or subgroups and define assessments for each responsibility
constraints: The authors caution the approach "is not just plug-and-play" and "requires large amounts of data"
target_learners: interdependent teams in military and civilian training settings
target_learning_goals: collective task performance
team coordination
individual competencies within team contexts
examples: Table 1 structures a football team's long-yardage play as a team concept with roles, responsibilities, shared knowledge, and assessments; Table 2 shows a DKF structure for the individual task of playing center
key_sources: J. D. Fletcher & Robert A. Sottilare. (2018). Shared Mental Models in Support of Adaptive Instruction for Teams Using the GIFT Tutoring Architecture. Int J Artif Intell Educ 28:265–285. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0147-y

article_title: The Effects of Geography Information System (GIS) Based Teaching on Underachieving Students' Mastery Goal and Achievement
citation: Soon Singh Bikar Singh, Balan Rathakrishnan, Sabariah Sharif, Rosy Talin, Oliver Valentine Eboy. (2016). The Effects of Geography Information System (GIS) Based Teaching on Underachieving Students' Mastery Goal and Achievement. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 15(4). https://www.tojet.net
title: GIS-based instruction unit built in ArcGIS 10.0 for the topic 'The Distribution of the Forests and Wildlife in the World'
description: An eight-lesson GIS-based instruction unit designed using ArcGIS 10.0 software, delivered in a computer laboratory for eight weeks with one 80-minute lesson weekly, plus two extra lessons introducing the GIS software. The article states the unit "focused on the topic of 'The Distribution of the Forests and Wildlife in the World'". Lesson activities focused on creating data, inserting hyperlinks, tracing forest areas, and comparing and labelling forest areas on world maps, with induction sets, classroom exercises, and question-and-answer segments.
requirements: Access to a computer laboratory and ArcGIS 10.0 software
Two extra introductory lessons to familiarise students with the GIS software before content teaching begins
constraints: Evaluated only with Form 4 (Grade 10) underachieving Geography students in two rural Smart Schools in Sabah
target_learners: Form 4 (Grade 10) underachieving secondary Geography students
target_learning_goals: Understanding the type and distribution of world forests and wildlife
Mastery goal orientation toward learning Geography
examples: Students traced, plotted and labelled their own forest maps and created hyperlink icons to add extra information about forests
A drag-and-drop activity in which students located wildlife symbols on the map according to the forest in which they live

article_title: The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment
citation: James Kim, Lowry Hemphill, Margaret Troyer, Stephanie Jones, Maria LaRusso, Ha-Yeon Kim, Suzanne Donovan, Catherine Snow. (2016). The Experimental Effects of the Strategic Adolescent Reading Intervention (STARI) on a Scenarios-Based Reading Comprehension Assessment. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract.
title: GISA: a 45-minute internet-delivered scenario-based reading comprehension assessment
description: The Global Integrated Scenario-Based Assessment (GISA), developed by ETS researchers, is a 45-minute, scenario-based assessment of reading comprehension delivered over the Internet. Students read a motivating scenario (e.g., building a class website on organic farming) and then read varied text types — informational passages, simulated web searches and discussions, cartoons, charts, and graphic organizers — to answer embedded questions, tapping integration of multiple text sources.
requirements: Internet delivery
Pretest administration for use as a covariate in impact models
target_learners: Middle school students
target_learning_goals: Evaluating and integrating information from multiple text sources
Scenario-based reading comprehension
examples: Sabatini et al. (2014) report Pearson correlations between r = .71 and r = .77 between the GISA and the six RISE subtests, which the authors cite as initial convergent validity evidence

article_title: Effectiveness of a Phonological Awareness Training Intervention on Word Recognition Ability of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
citation: Mohammed, A. A., & Mostafa, A. A. (2012). Effectiveness of a Phonological Awareness Training Intervention on Word recognition ability of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder. International Journal of Psycho-Educational Sciences, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Gillon's three-level taxonomy of phonological awareness: onset-rime, syllable, and phoneme awareness
description: The article describes phonological awareness as a general ability with multiple dimensions varying in difficulty, citing Gillon (2004) who "describes phonological awareness in terms of three different levels." These levels are onset-rime awareness, syllable awareness and phoneme awareness. Onset-rime awareness involves analyzing syllables into onset and rime units; syllable awareness is the ability to detect the smallest unit of speech that can be produced in isolation; phoneme awareness includes abilities to segment, rearrange, and substitute phonemes. The training program in this study incorporated this spectrum of PA skills.
requirements: Children must learn that words can be divided into segments of sound smaller than a syllable and learn about individual phonemes themselves
target_learners: children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
preschool and early elementary children
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness
reading readiness
examples: The training program's activities (sound matching, rhyming, blending, segmentation) were sequenced across this continuum from easiest to hardest.
key_sources: Mohammed, A. A., & Mostafa, A. A. (2012). Effectiveness of a Phonological Awareness Training Intervention on Word recognition ability of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder. International Journal of Psycho-Educational Sciences, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED579061

article_title: The Effect of Virtual vs. Traditional Classroom Instruction on Creative Thinking of Iranian High School EFL Learners
citation: Soheila Shafiee Varzaneh & Roya Baharlooie. (2015). The Effect of Virtual vs. Traditional Classroom Instruction on Creative Thinking of Iranian High School EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n5p177
title: Divergent thinking model of creative thinking measurement (Gilford)
description: The article operationalizes creative thinking through Gilford's divergent thinking framework, assessing four components: "originality, fluency, flexibility, and elaboration". Originality scores uncommon uses (1 point for responses given by 5% of the group, 2 points for 1%), fluency counts total responses, flexibility counts distinct categories covered, and elaboration scores level of detail. This model served as the study's main measurement instrument via the Gilford Alternative Uses Task.
requirements: Scoring requires group-level response frequency data to classify originality points
constraints: Measured via a single Alternative Uses Task question administered at pretest and posttest
target_learners: female Iranian high school EFL learners
target_learning_goals: creative thinking measurement
examples: Example scoring: 'Imitation mini-trombone' scored as more uncommon than 'holding papers together' for the word 'paper clip'
key_sources: Soheila Shafiee Varzaneh & Roya Baharlooie. (2015). The Effect of Virtual vs. Traditional Classroom Instruction on Creative Thinking of Iranian High School EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n5p177

article_title: The Impact of Consecutive Interpreting Training on the L2 Listening Competence Enhancement
citation: Tongtong Zhang & Zhiwei Wu. (2017). The Impact of Consecutive Interpreting Training on the L2 Listening Competence Enhancement. English Language Teaching, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n1p72
title: Gile's Effort Models of consecutive interpreting (comprehension and production phases)
description: Gile's model splits consecutive interpreting into two phases. In the comprehension phase, "interpreting=L+N+M+ C (L: listening and analysis, N: note-taking, M: short-term memory operations and C: coordination)", while the production phase is primarily target-speech production (Rem+Read+P+C). Each component occupies a portion of processing capacity, and listening and analysis is "the very first step leading to the success of CI". The article uses the model to explain why CI training pushes beginners to attend to every detail, improving intensive listening.
requirements: Excellent listening and analysis ability contributes to saving processing capacity, since note-taking takes up a large proportion of it in CI
constraints: The article notes "listening and analysis" in interpreting differs from L2 listening comprehension, focusing on analysis rather than meaning understanding and language acquisition
target_learners: undergraduate interpreting student beginners
target_learning_goals: consecutive interpreting performance
L2 listening competence
examples: The article uses the model to interpret students' questionnaire comments about straining to catch every word during CI exercises
key_sources: Tongtong Zhang & Zhiwei Wu. (2017). The Impact of Consecutive Interpreting Training on the L2 Listening Competence Enhancement. English Language Teaching, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n1p72

article_title: The Effects of Giving and Receiving Marginal L1 Glosses on L2 Vocabulary Learning by Upper Secondary Learners
citation: Hosein Vafadar Samian, Thomas Chow Voon Foo & Hassan Mohebbi. (2016). The Effects of Giving and Receiving Marginal L1 Glosses on L2 Vocabulary Learning by Upper Secondary Learners. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p66
title: Have learners give (produce) marginal L1 glosses rather than only receive them to maximize vocabulary-learning gains
description: The article's giver condition required learners to consult a bilingualized dictionary and write L1 equivalents for highlighted words, combining input-based glossing with output-based production. The authors explain the giver group's advantage by noting that output-based instruction highlights the efficacy of production tasks like translation in prompting L2 vocabulary learning. Giving glosses is therefore an implementable activity recipe for vocabulary lessons.
requirements: Targeted lexical items must be highlighted in authentic reading texts, with spaces provided for learners to write L1 equivalents, and a bilingualized dictionary available for consultation.
constraints: The treatment period was limited to three sessions which were relatively short; the sample size was smaller than wished for; word-frequency effects were not examined.
target_learners: upper secondary EFL learners (ages 15-17, intermediate level)
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary learning and retention of targeted lexical items
examples: Giver-group participants performed three reading comprehension tasks, consulted the bilingualized Longman dictionary, and wrote down their L1 equivalents in the spaces provided.
key_sources: Hosein Vafadar Samian, Thomas Chow Voon Foo & Hassan Mohebbi. (2016). The Effects of Giving and Receiving Marginal L1 Glosses on L2 Vocabulary Learning by Upper Secondary Learners. English Language Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n2p66

article_title: The formation of self-concept and intrinsic value in arts-related domains: Extending the generalized internal/external frame of reference model to music and visual arts.
citation: Arens, A. Katrin; Fiedler, Daniel; Hasselhorn, Johannes; Möller, Jens. (2025). The formation of self‐concept and intrinsic value in arts‐related domains: Extending the generalized internal/external frame of reference model to music and visual arts. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70038
title: Generalized internal/external frame of reference (GI/E) model extended to music and visual arts
description: The GI/E model extends the internal/external frame of reference model beyond self-concept to other motivational constructs and beyond math and verbal domains to other school subjects. It assumes two comparison processes shape domain-specific motivation: social comparisons within a domain, producing positive within-domain achievement–self-concept and achievement–intrinsic value relations, and dimensional comparisons across domains, producing negative (contrast) or positive (assimilation) cross-domain relations. This study applied it with eight domains including music and visual arts and tested self-concept as mediator of achievement–intrinsic value relations and gender invariance. The article defines intrinsic value as "students' liking and enjoyment of a subject".
requirements: Requires measures of achievement, domain-specific self-concept, and the motivational construct (e.g., intrinsic value) in multiple domains, analysed via structural equation modelling.
constraints: The observed pattern of relations "only indicates but does not prove the implementation and application of social and dimensional comparisons"; the model has been fully supported only in later elementary and secondary school.
target_learners: Secondary school students (Grades 7–9, academic track)
target_learning_goals: Formation of domain-specific academic self-concept and intrinsic value across school subjects including music and visual arts
examples: The study fitted a GI/E model with achievement, self-concept, and intrinsic value factors in eight domains (math, German, English, physics, biology, second foreign language, music, visual arts) using N = 442 students.
key_sources: Arens, A. Katrin; Fiedler, Daniel; Hasselhorn, Johannes; Möller, Jens. (2025). The formation of self‐concept and intrinsic value in arts‐related domains: Extending the generalized internal/external frame of reference model to music and visual arts. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70038

article_title: Factors Influencing ICU Nurses' Proficiency in Point-of-Care Gastrointestinal Ultrasound: A National Cross-Sectional Study.
citation: Wang Gang, Liu Yingying, Wang Shengyun, Gao Silong, Lin Hui, Wu Qian, Huang Debin, Pan Yueshuai, Zhao Yuxiao, Wei Huimin, Wei Lili. (2026). Factors Influencing ICU Nurses’ Proficiency in Point‐of‐Care Gastrointestinal Ultrasound: A National Cross‐Sectional Study. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/3178958
title: GI-POCUS proficiency as an organizational capability shaped by leadership, training governance, and workflow integration
description: The article frames nurses' GI-POCUS proficiency not as an isolated individual skill but as an organizational capability: it states proficiency "should be understood as an organizational capability shaped by leadership engagement, training governance, and workflow integration, rather than as an isolated technical skill." Under this account, departmental structures — SOPs, quality control, mentorship, billing recognition, documentation systems, and embedded routine workflows — jointly determine whether nurses acquire and sustain competency. The survey data showing billability, documentation, and workflow integration as independent predictors are offered as support.
requirements: Organizational governance mechanisms including SOPs, quality control systems, and documentation of findings within nursing records
Leadership engagement and institutional recognition mechanisms such as performance evaluation or billing policies
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional survey data from China; the authors state findings on billing policies and institutional support may not be directly generalizable to other healthcare systems
target_learners: ICU nurses learning point-of-care gastrointestinal ultrasound
target_learning_goals: Acquiring and sustaining GI-POCUS psychomotor and image-interpretation skills for enteral nutrition management and GI dysfunction detection
examples: In the survey, 83.2% of units lacked SOPs, 67.0% had no quality control mechanism, 69.7% lacked a mentorship system, and 84.4% could not bill for GI-POCUS examinations, which the authors call a "permitted but unregulated" managerial gap
key_sources: Wang Gang, Liu Yingying, Wang Shengyun, Gao Silong, Lin Hui, Wu Qian, Huang Debin, Pan Yueshuai, Zhao Yuxiao, Wei Huimin, Wei Lili. (2026). Factors Influencing ICU Nurses’ Proficiency in Point‐of‐Care Gastrointestinal Ultrasound: A National Cross‐Sectional Study. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/3178958

article_title: Structured reflective sessions enhance knowledge and clinical skills in operating room technology students: a Solomon four-group study.
citation: Hassani Nia Nasser, Karami Sahar, Shahraki Farimah, Kohan Mahmoud. (2025). Structured reflective sessions enhance knowledge and clinical skills in operating room technology students: a Solomon four-group study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08431-w
title: Gibbs' reflective cycle integrated with Kolb's experiential learning theory as the framework for structured reflective sessions
description: The article grounds its intervention in Gibbs' six-stage reflective cycle — "description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, and action plan" — which "collectively support systematic learning from clinical experiences". Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory supplies a complementary four-stage cycle (Concrete Experience, Reflective Observation, Abstract Conceptualization, Active Experimentation) that the authors use to interpret how clinical encounters are transformed into knowledge and skills. The intervention operationalized both: guided prompts supported Reflective Observation, structured templates supported Abstract Conceptualization, and DOPS improvement was read as Active Experimentation.
requirements: Trained facilitators with structured, immediate feedback; reflection templates, scenarios and facilitator guides for consistency
constraints: The authors note novices require more scaffolding and guided reflection than advanced students, per the Dreyfus model discussion
target_learners: undergraduate operating room technology students (3rd and 5th semesters)
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge of circulating nurse and surgical techniques
procedural clinical skills
professional self-awareness and reflective habits
examples: A 120-minute workshop in week 5 followed by five weekly 90-minute small-group reflective sessions and at least two individual written reflections during clinical placement
key_sources: Hassani Nia Nasser, Karami Sahar, Shahraki Farimah, Kohan Mahmoud. (2025). Structured reflective sessions enhance knowledge and clinical skills in operating room technology students: a Solomon four-group study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08431-w

article_title: Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Hands-On Simulation Case for Internal Medicine Residents Improves Knowledge and Confidence.
citation: Wilkoff MH, Seltzer ES, Piniella NR, Seepersaud H, Loanzon P, Kurtz S, Salonia J, Jodorkovsky D. (2025). Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Hands-On Simulation Case for Internal Medicine Residents Improves Knowledge and Confidence. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11541
title: GI bleed hands-on simulation case using a SimMan 3G manikin with moulage, confederates, and a 30–40 minute lecture-based debrief
description: A case-based simulation in which a 45-year-old male with alcohol use disorder, hematemesis, and hemodynamic instability deteriorates via changing vital signs, requiring residents to resuscitate, order medications and transfusion, and consult GI and ICU. The setup used a "SimMan 3G Manikin" with "moulage hematemesis" and moulage melena, confederate roles (RN, GI fellow, critical care physician), and a 30–40 minute debrief with a PowerPoint lecture covering EV, PUD, central venous access, massive transfusion protocol, and hemorrhagic shock.
requirements: Simulation faculty and content-expert faculty involvement, plus complex simulation equipment including a code cart and manikin
constraints: The authors note the simulation "required significant faculty involvement and availability as well as complex simulation equipment, which could be a constraining factor for institutions with limited faculty or equipment"
target_learners: Internal medicine residents (PGY1–PGY3)
target_learning_goals: Managing upper GI bleeds: differential diagnosis, resuscitation, medical management, endoscopy timing, and discharge planning
examples: Sessions ran Tuesdays and Thursdays over an 8-week period, 1 hour each with four to six residents, used 16 times during the 2023–2024 academic year
key_sources: Wilkoff MH, Seltzer ES, Piniella NR, Seepersaud H, Loanzon P, Kurtz S, Salonia J, Jodorkovsky D. (2025). Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Hands-On Simulation Case for Internal Medicine Residents Improves Knowledge and Confidence. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11541

article_title: Enhancing secondary school students' science process skills through guided inquiry-based laboratory activities in biology.
citation: Chengere Ashebir Mekonnen, Bono Beyene Dobo, Zinabu Samuel Assefa, Jilo Kedir Woliy. (2025). Enhancing secondary school students’ science process skills through guided inquiry-based laboratory activities in biology. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320692
title: GIBLEI: Guided Inquiry-Based Laboratory Experiments enriched Instructional approach
description: GIBLEI is an instructional approach that integrates hands-on laboratory experimentation with guided inquiry, in which students "investigate, hypothesize, experiment, and draw conclusions" through an eight-stage cycle from semi-structured problems to assessment. It is grounded in constructivism, cognitive apprenticeship, and self-determination theory, using scaffolded teacher facilitation, collaborative design discussions, and reflective conclusions. The article positions it as a response to resource constraints in Ethiopian secondary schools, incorporating locally available materials and structured teacher support.
requirements: Teacher training in inquiry-based pedagogy and the 5E lesson plan format, as provided in the study's three-day training program
Scaffolded teacher and lab-technician facilitation across the eight-stage activity cycle
constraints: Developed and tested in resource-limited Ethiopian secondary schools; the open-ended nature of inquiry can cause cognitive overload without sufficient foundational knowledge
target_learners: Grade 10 secondary school biology students
target_learning_goals: Science process skills: formulating hypotheses, designing experiments, interpreting data, and drawing conclusions
examples: Over eight weeks, EG lessons followed an eight-stage GIBLEI procedure structured into the 5E lesson plan format, with guided inquiry activities concentrated in the exploration phase.
key_sources: Chengere Ashebir Mekonnen, Bono Beyene Dobo, Zinabu Samuel Assefa, Jilo Kedir Woliy. (2025). Enhancing secondary school students’ science process skills through guided inquiry-based laboratory activities in biology. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320692

article_title: The effect of interactive learning methods and reflection on nurses' learning in patient safety at the ICU and Emergency department.
citation: Mirzaei Samaneh, Keshmiri Fatemeh, Norouzinia Roohangiz, Mirjalili Najmeh, Baghshahi Naeimeh, Gholinataj Jelodar Mohsen. (2025). The effect of interactive learning methods and reflection on nurses' learning in patient safety at the ICU and Emergency department. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12320-9
title: Gibbs reflective cycle as a structured reflection intervention for patient safety learning
description: The article operationalised the reflection intervention using the Gibbs model, a six-stage reflective cycle comprising "initial experience, description, feeling, evaluation, analysis, general conclusion, remarkable conclusion, and individual action plan". Participants answered structured questions about what happened, their thoughts and feelings, good and bad aspects, lessons learned, alternative actions, and future responses, then shared reflections with peers and a facilitator who summarised the discussion. The article frames reflection as a means of breaking automatic habits and reducing errors.
requirements: Proper guidance and training in reflection to engage in deeper learning
Structured questions guiding each stage of the cycle
Facilitator-led summarising of group discussion
constraints: In this study reflection did not significantly outperform lecture on attitude (p = 0.309) or practice (p = 0.064); the authors suggest lack of guidance in deeper reflection may explain the null result
target_learners: Practising nurses in critical care and emergency settings
target_learning_goals: Learning from experience to avoid repeating mistakes
Reducing automatic, unconscious errors in patient care
examples: Nurses completed the six-stage cycle on safety-error experiences, shared thoughts in the final stage, and received peer and facilitator feedback
key_sources: Mirzaei Samaneh, Keshmiri Fatemeh, Norouzinia Roohangiz, Mirjalili Najmeh, Baghshahi Naeimeh, Gholinataj Jelodar Mohsen. (2025). The effect of interactive learning methods and reflection on nurses' learning in patient safety at the ICU and Emergency department. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12320-9

article_title: A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown.
citation: Gallardo-Alba Cristóbal, Grüning Björn, Serrano-Solano Beatriz. (2021). A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown. PLoS Computational Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008922
title: Git with GitHub and GitHub Classroom as collaborative learning tools for methodological skills
description: Git with the GitHub hosting service is presented as an educational tool for 'the development of methodological skills'. Its Pull Request mechanism lets users 'request, review, and discuss changes to be made in the content of a project', enabling a participatory culture; GitHub classroom adds repository distribution and working-group organisation through a web interface.
requirements: Its success as a collaborative learning tool rests on its being 'the de facto platform for open-source projects, allowing the students to collaborate in real-life scenarios'.
constraints: The article notes that 'GitHub was not designed as an LMS', so complementary tools were developed for course functions.
target_learners: computer science and bioinformatics students working in groups
target_learning_goals: development of methodological skills
collaboration in real-life open-source scenarios
examples: GitHub classroom 'facilitates the distribution of repositories and the organization of working groups through the use of a web interface'.
key_sources: Gallardo-Alba Cristóbal, Grüning Björn, Serrano-Solano Beatriz. (2021). A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown. PLoS Computational Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008922

article_title: Task Monitoring and Working Memory as Executive Components Predictive of General and Specific Academic Achievements in 6-9-Year-Old Children.
citation: Quílez-Robres A., Moyano N., Cortés-Pascual A. (2021). Task Monitoring and Working Memory as Executive Components Predictive of General and Specific Academic Achievements in 6–9-Year-Old Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18136681
title: Gioia et al.'s three-index model of executive functions (behavioral, emotional, and cognitive regulation) measured by the BRIEF-2
description: The article adopts Gioia et al.'s model in which executive functions form "a multifactorial structure" organized into three indices—behavioral regulation (inhibition, self-monitoring), emotional regulation (flexibility, emotional control), and cognitive regulation (initiative, working memory, planning, task supervision, organization of materials)—combined into a global executive function index. It is operationalized through the BRIEF-2 questionnaire, a 63-item parent-rated frequency scale where high scores indicate problems in the corresponding area. The study uses this structure to test which index predicts academic achievement at ages 6–9.
requirements: Administered as a questionnaire answered by parents, teachers, or caregivers of the children being evaluated
constraints: High scores indicate problems, so correlations with achievement are negative in this study
target_learners: Children aged 6–9 in elementary education
target_learning_goals: General academic achievement
Language Arts achievement
Mathematics achievement
examples: The study administered the Spanish adaptation of the BRIEF-2 family version to parents of 133 children and found the cognitive regulation index scales carried the predictive weight.
key_sources: Quílez-Robres A., Moyano N., Cortés-Pascual A. (2021). Task Monitoring and Working Memory as Executive Components Predictive of General and Specific Academic Achievements in 6–9-Year-Old Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18136681
